value.overview: The Dot-winged Antwren (Microrhopias quixensis) is a small Neotropical antbird found from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America. It is usually encountered in pairs or small family groups, often moving actively through dense vegetation. Despite its name, it is not dependent on army ants; it mainly searches foliage and vines for arthropods. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of suitable lowland and foothill forest habitats.
value.classification: The Dot-winged Antwren belongs to the antbird family Thamnophilidae and the subfamily Thamnophilinae. It is the only species in the genus Microrhopias.
value.identification: This small, active antwren has a short tail, a slim bill, and contrasting plumage. Adult males are mainly blackish or dark gray, with conspicuous pale or whitish spots on the wing coverts and often pale edging in the wings. Females and immature birds are generally browner or gray-brown and less strongly contrasted, but still show the spotted-wing pattern. It frequently flicks its wings and moves quickly through tangled vegetation, making its distinctive wing markings useful during brief views.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a broad distribution from southern Mexico through Central America and southward into northern and central South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, including eastern and central-southern parts of the country, generally in lowlands and foothills. It uses tropical evergreen and semi-deciduous forest, secondary growth, forest edges, clearings, vine tangles, and sometimes shaded cacao or guava plantations. It usually favors dense, structurally complex vegetation rather than the interior of unbroken mature forest.
value.migrationStatus: The Dot-winged Antwren is considered a year-round resident, including in Costa Rica. It does not undertake regular long-distance migration, although local movements may occur when birds follow changing food or vegetation conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited across much of the range. In Costa Rica, nesting activity has been reported from January through August, covering much of the dry and early wet seasons. As in related antwrens, pairs defend small territories and use dense vegetation for nesting. The nest is a small, enclosed or partially enclosed structure placed low among twigs, stems, or tangled plants. Both adults are expected to participate in territory defense and care of the young.
value.dietFeeding: The Dot-winged Antwren feeds mainly on arthropods, including insects and other small invertebrates. It usually forages in pairs or small family groups, often between roughly one and several meters above the ground. Birds glean prey from leaves, stems, vines, and small branches while hopping, hanging, reaching, or briefly hovering. They may join mixed-species feeding flocks temporarily but generally remain associated with their own pair or family group.
value.behavior: This antwren is highly active and often difficult to follow as it moves through dense foliage. It commonly travels in pairs or small family groups and maintains contact with soft calls while searching for prey. It may participate briefly in mixed-species flocks, especially along forest edges and in secondary vegetation. Army-ant swarms are not central to its feeding strategy, though individuals may occasionally take advantage of prey disturbed near a swarm. Wing flicking and rapid movements are characteristic behaviors.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is believed to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
